title: Peter and Cornelius: The Spirit Falls on Gentiles
summary: An angel tells Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea who worships Israel's God, to send for Peter. At Joppa, Peter sees a vision of a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice telling him not to call impure what God has made clean. He goes to Cornelius's house, preaches Jesus, and while he is still speaking the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners, who are then baptized.
story: Jesus told the apostles they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The first two circles have already been reached: Pentecost in Jerusalem, Philip in Samaria, and Peter traveling among the towns of the coast in chapter 9, where he raised Tabitha at Joppa. This chapter opens the third circle. Luke tells it at great length and then has Peter retell it in chapter 11 and refer to it again in chapter 15, which is his way of saying that this is one of the hinges of the whole book. The question it answers is simple and enormous: can a person who is not Jewish belong fully to the people of Israel's Messiah without first becoming Jewish? Everything that follows, including Paul's missions, depends on the answer God gives in this house in Caesarea.
historical:
Caesarea, on the Mediterranean coast about 30 miles (50 kilometers) north of Joppa, was a largely Gentile city built by Herod the Great and named for Caesar Augustus, with an artificial harbor, a theater, and a temple to Rome and Augustus. It served as the seat of the Roman governors of Judea, which is why a Roman officer would be stationed there. The episode probably falls in the late 30s or early 40s AD, though Acts gives no date. Luke calls Cornelius a centurion, an officer nominally commanding a hundred men (in practice often about eighty), in the Italian Regiment, or cohort. An inscription attests an Italian cohort in Syria later in the first century; whether the same unit was in Caesarea at this time is uncertain, and scholars differ on how to fit the detail.

Joppa (modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv) was an old Jewish port town. Peter stays there with Simon, a tanner, whose trade involved handling the hides of dead animals and was regarded by some later Jewish sources as unpleasant and ritually troublesome. That Peter lodges with him may already show him loosening his grip on some purity boundaries before the vision comes.
cultural:
Cornelius is what Luke calls devout and God-fearing: a Gentile drawn to the God of Israel who prays, gives to the poor, and respects the Jewish people, but who has not been circumcised or converted. Such God-fearers were found around synagogues throughout the empire. He prays at the ninth hour (about three in the afternoon), the hour of the afternoon offering at the temple and a regular time of Jewish prayer. Peter prays at the sixth hour (about noon) on a flat roof, which in that world served as extra living space.

The vision draws on the food laws of Leviticus 11, which divided animals into clean (permitted to eat) and unclean (forbidden). These laws were one of the most visible marks separating Jews from Gentiles, and meals were where the separation was felt most. Peter's words in verse 28 reflect that: many Jews avoided eating in Gentile homes, where food would not be prepared by Jewish rules and might have been offered to idols. The practice varied, and the law of Moses nowhere forbids entering a Gentile house, but the social wall was real. Peter draws the conclusion himself: the vision is about more than menus, since God has shown him that he should not call any man impure or unclean.
literary: Luke builds the chapter out of two visions that interlock, one to a Gentile and one to a Jew, each prepared without the other's knowledge, so that when they meet both can see God has arranged it. Repetition carries the argument: the vision happens three times, Cornelius's angel is described twice (verses 3-6 and 30-32), and the whole account will be retold in 11:1-18. The chapter moves from Caesarea to Joppa and back, and its climax is an interruption: Peter's sermon (verses 34-43), a compact summary of the gospel from John's baptism to the resurrection and the coming judgment, is cut short when the Spirit falls. The ending mirrors Pentecost, with speaking in tongues and praise, so that no one can say these Gentiles received something lesser.

outline.t: Peter's vision of the sheet at Joppa
The messengers arrive and the Spirit sends Peter
Peter preaches Jesus, Lord of all
The Spirit falls and the Gentiles are baptized

doctrines.note: Peter's sermon ends with the promise that everyone who believes in Jesus receives forgiveness of sins through His name (verse 43). The Spirit's coming on uncircumcised Gentiles shows that this salvation is received by faith, not by first taking on the marks of Jewish identity.

The Spirit directs every step: he speaks to Peter (verse 19), and he falls on the listeners before anyone has decided what to do with them. The church does not extend the gospel to the Gentiles on its own initiative; it follows where God has already gone.

The gospel is here called the message of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all (verse 36). The word all governs the chapter: no nation is outside the reach of the good news, and no one can be written off as unclean.

words.note: Koinos, common. In ordinary Greek it means shared or public, but among Greek-speaking Jews it came to mean profane or ritually defiled, the opposite of holy. Peter's objection pairs it with akathartos, unclean. The vision overturns the category: what God has cleansed, Peter may not call common.

Prosopoleptes, one who shows favoritism, literally one who receives a face, that is, judges by appearance or status. The word is rare and appears only here in the New Testament, though related words are used by Paul and James. Peter's discovery that God is not such a person echoes the Old Testament conviction that God does not show partiality (Deuteronomy 10:17).

Phobeo, to fear. Cornelius is described as one who fears God, a standard way of naming a Gentile worshiper of Israel's God, and Peter picks up the phrase when he says God welcomes those from every nation who fear Him (verse 35). The fear meant is reverent worship, not terror.

christ: Peter's sermon is a short gospel in itself: Jesus of Nazareth, anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and with power, went around doing good and healing, was put to death by hanging on a tree (an echo of Deuteronomy 21:22-23, where one hanged on a tree is under a curse), was raised on the third day, and was seen by chosen witnesses who ate and drank with him. He is now appointed as judge of the living and the dead, and the prophets testify that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name. The chapter shows what that title Lord of all means in practice. Jesus is not a Jewish Messiah whom Gentiles may admire from a distance. He is Lord of Cornelius's household as fully as of Peter's, and his Spirit comes to both alike.

hard.q: If God already accepted Cornelius's prayers and gifts, why did he need to hear about Jesus?
hard.a:
Verse 4 says Cornelius's prayers and gifts rose as a memorial offering before God, and verse 35 says God welcomes those from every nation who fear Him. Read alone, those lines could suggest that sincere devotion is enough. But the angel's whole purpose is to send Cornelius to Peter, and in 11:14 Peter reports that the message would be one by which you and all your household will be saved. Most interpreters therefore read Cornelius as someone God was drawing, whose seeking God honored by sending him the gospel, rather than someone already saved without it.

Christians differ on what this implies for people who never hear of Christ. Some emphasize that God answered Cornelius's faith with fuller revelation, and hold that he does so for any genuine seeker. Others hold that God's acceptance in verse 35 refers to his willingness to receive people of any nation, not to their standing before hearing the gospel. Both readings agree on what the chapter plainly teaches: God has no favorite ethnicity, and forgiveness comes through the name of Jesus.

questions: Peter needed a vision repeated three times before he would enter a Gentile's house. What boundaries do Christians today treat as God's when they may simply be custom?
Cornelius gathered his relatives and close friends to hear Peter. Who would you want in the room if you expected to hear a word from God?
The Spirit interrupted Peter's sermon. What does it say about the church's mission that God often moves ahead of his people's plans?
